Alcohol. An organic compound in which a hydroxyl functional group—that's OH—is bonded to a saturated carbon atom. The hydroxyl group is highly polar, which means alcohols can participate in intermolecular hydrogen bonding. That gives them significantly higher boiling points and greater water solubility than their corresponding hydrocarbons.

Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary, or tertiary based on how many carbon atoms are bonded to the carbon bearing the hydroxyl group. This classification dictates their reactivity and oxidation pathways. Short-chain alcohols like methanol and ethanol are soluble in water because of hydrogen bonding, but as the hydrophobic carbon chain gets longer, water solubility decreases.

There are several ways to synthesize alcohols. You can hydrate alkenes using acid-catalyzed hydration or oxymercuration-demercuration to get Markovnikov products, or hydroboration-oxidation to get anti-Markovnikov products. Alternatively, you can reduce carbonyls. Aldehydes and ketones are reduced using sodium borohydride, while carboxylic acids and esters require the stronger lithium aluminum hydride.

Primary alcohols oxidize to aldehydes under mild oxidants like PCC, or to carboxylic acids under strong oxidants like the Jones reagent. Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones. Alcohols also undergo dehydration in the presence of strong acid catalysts like sulfuric acid, forming alkenes through an elimination reaction. They react with carboxylic acids in Fischer esterification, which produces esters. Alcohols are among the most versatile intermediates in synthetic chemistry, widely used as solvents, fuels, and chemical precursors.

Carboxylic acids condense with alcohols to form esters, and oxidation of primary alcohols yields carboxylic acids. Alcohols and ethers are constitutional isomers with the same molecular formula, like ethanol and dimethyl ether. Primary alcohols can be mildly oxidized to yield aldehydes. Secondary alcohols, when oxidized, yield ketones. And structurally, an alcohol can be thought of as a water molecule with one hydrogen replaced by an alkyl group.
